newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China regains appetite for East Asian crude oil.
newsitem.headline: China regains appetite for East Asian crude oil.

text.p: China, the world's fastest growing oil consuming country, has regained appetite for East Asian crudes, notably Indonesian and Vietnamese, after a four-month long diet, traders said on Monday.
They said China had bought as much as 1.2 million barrels of Vietnamese Bach Ho crude and between 1.0 and 1.5 million barrels of Indonesian Minas crude for September liftings.
In August, China was estimated to have bought about 550,000 barrels of Minas as well as plenty of Oman and West African crudes. On average China buys up to one million barrels of Minas a month.
China's recent purchases of Minas have helped to boost the crude's price to about a 15-cent discount to the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP) from a heavy discount of 70 cents in mid-August.

Some traders were surprised China was willing to pay a 15-cent discount, but others said China would be willing to buy as long as prices remained under the ICP, particularly because Middle East and West African cargoes have been firming.

In addition, only 200,000-300,000 barrels of September Minas were left for September liftings, unless Pertamina's Japanese affiliates asked for 500,000 barrels in additional allocation, a Minas producer said.
"It (the 15-cent discount) is a good price for sellers," a trader said. "But China has to come out to buy because they have been putting off their purchases for a while."
Another trader said Chinese refineries were in need of Minas-grade crudes.

Traders said the spike in international crude prices following the U.S. missile strikes on Iraq last week could have been one reason China decided to buy now, believing prices could rise further later because of the Middle East tension.
Traders said Minas would be an attractive buy for China so long as prompt West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude continued to hover over $23.00 and Brent, plus Brent-related crudes, remained firm.
Prompt NYMEX crude rose as high as $24.25 after the U.S. strike against Iraq, while prompt Brent jumped to $23.50. They ended last week at $23.85 to $22.54 respectively.
Minas is now quoted near $20.00 per barrel compared with $19.49 for August liftings.
Traders said firm western crude prices could attract Far East crudes out of the region.

This happened in August when very low values of Minas and slow demand in Asia prompted two majors to ship about one million barrels of Minas and another million barrels of Indonesian Attaka and Bontang Mix to the United States.
Traders said the option remained open for sellers to ship Indonesian crudes westward in September. One producer said 500,000-700,000 barrels of Minas could be shipped to the U.S. West Coast.

However, another trader said buyers of Indonesian crudes would be wise to hold further purchases until October as the scheduled shutdown of the 125,000-barrel-per-day Balongan refinery next month would see a glut in Minas and Duri supplies.
Balongan processes 80 percent Duri and 20 percent Minas crudes.
